Depends on how "large scale changes" are defined. I will do my best to keep the users informed well in advance of changes which affect all users. Privacy Policy updates and updates to User Agreement will be announced and explained (in ELI5 tone?) well in advance.

When it comes to changing the architecture (APIs etc), this will be worked out with third party app/plugin/website developers in order to prevent any downtime to their services.

Currently, whoaverse is in very early alpha stage and we can not announce every change before it is made. However, we are keeping a close eye on /v/ideasforwhoaverse, open issues on whoaverse github repository and /v/whoaversedev in order to keep an open communication line with the community and prevent any catastrophic changes that people would not like.

But, on topic, I think the admin has the right to do whatever he wants. It's his site, his server. He invited us to play in his playground. This is a dude with a server... not an independent nation state.

If he wants to attract traffic then he'll implement sensible policies that the majority of the users like. (If not, there will be a mass exodus just like Reddit). You can please some of the people some of the time.

Maybe "rights" is too strong a term; they're hardly comparable to constitutional rights, as you point out. But since arranging a mass-exodus is costly and inconvenient, I think it's reasonable to hope that the admin(s) will strive to provide the best possible service for the users, not merely one which won't trigger a mass-exodus. Because of network effects, it's possible for a site to persist for a long time at a merely local maximum; in my option, this site should aspire to find the global maximum (insofar as such can be defined).

I agree with you about not making drastic changes on a whim. If there's a security reason for a quick fix then so be it. But, any sort of large-scale change to the API should be introduced to developers in advance so they can update their plugins and reduce the amount of annoyed users. When organizations get big and powerful, (e.g., Google or Reddit) they think they can do whatever they want. But, customers pay attention to that sort of thing and once it gets to be too much, they leave. This is why having competition is a good thing.

I think most important is communication between the admins in the users.
